text: So far you've worked with one value at a time. Real data comes in batches — many rows, many customers, many fields. This lesson covers three collection types: lists, tuples, and sets, and how to tell which one is the right tool for a given job.

A list holds multiple values in order, and you can add, remove, or change them after creation. Append adds a new value to the end, and you can grab any item by index — including negative indexing, where minus one means the last item. That comes up constantly once you're working with real batches of records.

A tuple looks like a list but uses parentheses, and once created it can't be changed — trying to reassign an item raises a TypeError. Why want something you can't change? Because it signals intent: a fixed, complete record. A common real use is a function returning more than one value, like this min-and-max helper handing back a tuple.

A set automatically removes duplicates and has no guaranteed order — it's the right tool whenever the question is "what are the distinct values here." Six repeated customer IDs become a set of three unique ones. This is a real, common question: how many distinct customers placed these orders, not how many order rows exist.

So: reach for a list when you're holding a batch of rows you might add to or remove from. Reach for a tuple for one fixed record, or when a function needs to hand back more than one value. And reach for a set the moment the question becomes "what's distinct here," or you need a fast membership check.

Lists, tuples, sets — three shapes for more than one value. But a single real-world record, like one row of an order, isn't really a list of unlabeled values. Next lesson: dictionaries, the key-value shape behind every JSON response, database row, and record you'll touch from here on.
